title: Earth's Temporary 'Second Moon': 2-Meter Asteroid 2026 QQ8 to Drift Away in Early December

content:
A roughly 2-meter-diameter asteroid, 2026 QQ8, has been captured by Earth's gravity since April and is orbiting the planet, and is expected to escape Earth's gravitational sphere and return to a solar orbit in early December. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center gave the object its official designation in late October. When first discovered, it was difficult to distinguish from satellite debris, but follow-up observations confirmed it is a natural object. Its closest approach to Earth is about 570,000 km, so there is no risk of collision, and even if it entered the atmosphere, most of it would burn up. Astronomers estimate that, on average, about one minimoon exists around Earth at any given time.

A "second moon" orbiting Earth has been confirmed. An asteroid just over 2 meters in diameter has been captured by Earth's gravity and has been circling the planet for several weeks, and is expected to escape Earth's gravitational sphere in early December.

The International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center (MPC) gave the object its official designation, "2026 QQ8," in late October. Krisztián Sárneczky, a research coordinator at Hungary's Konkoly Observatory, first discovered it in August, when it carried the provisional designation "Sar2901." Immediately after the discovery, it appeared no different from previously observed near-Earth asteroids, but precise orbital calculations revealed that it had been captured by Earth's gravity. Earth is believed to have captured the object in April.

Among near-Earth objects (NEOs), 2026 QQ8 belongs to the category of "minimoons"—natural objects temporarily captured by Earth. Minimoon is not a formally recognized academic term, but it is an expression astronomers have conventionally used to refer to objects that remain in Earth's orbit for a short period. Past examples include 2006 RH120, which orbited Earth for about a year, and 2020 CD3, which circled Earth over about three years.

Confirming the identity of this object took considerable time. Because it is so small and faint, it was difficult to distinguish from defunct satellites or their debris using visual or optical observations alone. Astronomers only leaned toward a natural origin after tracking the effect of solar radiation on the object's motion for several weeks, and follow-up observations using the Lowell Discovery Telescope in Arizona and a 2.2-meter telescope at Hawaii's Mauna Kea Observatory ultimately confirmed that it is a natural object, not artificial.

2026 QQ8 is not expected to collide with Earth. During its capture, its closest approach to Earth is estimated at about 570,000 km, farther than the average Earth-Moon distance of about 380,000 km. Even if it entered Earth's atmosphere, its small size means most of it would burn up and break apart without causing significant damage. Matthew Payne, director of the MPC, said it would amount to "at most a bright meteor appearing in the sky and a small booming sound."

Minimoons are by no means a rare phenomenon. "On average, there is probably about one minimoon around Earth at any given time," Payne said, explaining that "some stay for weeks to months, sometimes there are none at all, and sometimes two or so exist at the same time." The reason records are sparse is that most are extremely small and either far from Earth or moving at high speed, making them very difficult to detect with current observation systems.

Research is ongoing into the exact origin of 2026 QQ8. Most near-Earth objects are believed to originate from the asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. This region contains millions of rocky bodies of varying sizes orbiting the Sun, and gravitational interactions over millions of years are thought to have shifted some of them into orbits toward the inner solar system. Payne explained that when a near-Earth object approaches at a speed too slow to simply pass by, it can be influenced by the gravity of Earth and the Moon, gradually deviate from its original orbit, and enter an orbit around Earth.

Astronomers have identified about 40,000 near-Earth objects to date, while roughly 1.5 million objects have been cataloged across the entire solar system. That number is expected to grow substantially as observation capacity expands. Chile's Vera C. Rubin Observatory is carrying out the 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) project using a telescope equipped with the world's largest digital camera. Payne predicted that once the project is fully operational, the number of detectable objects will expand from the current 1.5 million to around 5 million.

This case is significant in that it has once again confirmed the existence of small objects that pass in and out of Earth's gravitational sphere. As observation technology advances, the frequency of minimoon detections is expected to rise further, providing basic data needed to understand the orbits and origins of near-Earth objects.
